extracted.intended_audience: educated British public, lawmakers, and political reformers (late 18th century)
extracted.subtask_description: A conservative political essay arguing for preserving ancient constitutional principles and warning against radical revolution; addresses the proper composition of representative bodies and the conditions under which forcible removal of rulers might be justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revolution as last resource
rubrics_metrics.description: “a revolution will be the very last resource of the thinking and the good.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revolution is an extraordinary question of state, outside ordinary law; it should be considered only when government is abused and deranged and the future prospect is as bad as the past. The speculative line where obedience ends and resistance begins is 'faint, obscure, and not easily definable' and is determined by dispositions, means, and probable consequences rather than by positive rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dethroning a monarch is an extra-legal, forceful act
rubrics_metrics.description: “The ceremony of cashiering kings... can rarely, if ever, be performed without force. It then becomes a case of war, and not of constitution.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deposing a king is a matter of war/force and not an ordinary constitutional process; laws and tribunals are ineffective amidst arms. Such measures are governed by considerations of dispositions, means, and probable consequences rather than legal entitlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer constitutional safeguards over deposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliamentary oversight, impeachment by the Commons, and the Declaration of Right are 'infinitely a better security' than the 'reservation of a right... often so mischievous' as cashiering governors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Security for liberty should rest on institutional checks (constant inspection of Parliament, impeachment) and statutory limits rather than on difficult, uncertain, and dangerous practices of deposing rulers.

rubrics_metrics.name: King is sovereign, not a removable servant
rubrics_metrics.description: Although 'kings... are undoubtedly the servants of the people' in one sense, 'the law... calls this high-magistrate... "our sovereign lord the king"' and our Constitution makes no provision for rendering him responsible like a servant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the constitution described, the monarch is not subject to ordinary processes of accountability akin to those for servants; legal forms and titles reflect a sovereign status that resists servant-like removability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberties should be claimed as inherited (entailment) not abstract rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Our Constitution has uniformly claimed and asserted liberties as an 'entailed inheritance derived to us from our forefathers' rather than as vague 'rights of men.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political claims should appeal to historical precedent, hereditary transmission, and recorded rights (Magna Charta, Petition of Right, Declaration of Right) rather than abstract, speculative formulations that risk unsettling property and order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reforms must proceed by reference to antiquity and analogical precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: All reformation 'proceeded upon the principle of reference to antiquity' and 'will be carefully formed upon analogical precedent, authority, and example.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New laws and changes should be made by analogy to past institutions and authorities; the fabrication of a wholly new government is condemned as dangerous and ill-suited to national temper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assemblies should be composed of persons of permanent property, education, and stable habits
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing can secure a steady and moderate conduct in such assemblies, but that 'the body of them should be respectably composed, in point of condition in life, of permanent property, of education, and of such habits as enlarge and liberalize the understanding.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To secure sobriety and moderation in legislation, representatives should have stable property interests, education, and formative habits that enable them to judge rather than merely agitate or litigate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dominance by lawyers and litigious practitioners
rubrics_metrics.description: The Assembly's great proportion composed of practitioners in the law—'inferior, unlearned, mechanical, merely instrumental' members—predicts a dominion of chicane and litigious constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a representative body is dominated by lawyers and petty legal functionaries, their habits (litigiousness, local chicane) predispose the body toward unstable, opportunistic, and property-undermining measures rather than sober statesmanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid assemblies whose numerical structure allows easy concentration of power
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tiers État of six hundred persons, equal in number to the other two orders and then 'melted down into one', made it easy that 'a very small desertion from either of the other two orders must throw the power of both into the hands of the third.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representation rules and numerical composition matter: assemblies that merge orders or give parity in numbers without appropriate balancing safeguards risk sudden concentration of sovereign power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundations of liberty require religion and austere, masculine morality
rubrics_metrics.description: All other nations 'have laid the foundations of civil freedom in severer manners, and a system of a more austere and masculine morality.' France, by abandoning religion and discipline, 'doubled the license of a ferocious dissoluteness in manners.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stable freedom is tied to moral and religious restraints; abandoning these foundations fosters licentiousness and undermines civil order and institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect property rights and conventional credit as pillars of the state
rubrics_metrics.description: The subversion of the 'principle of property' produced national bankruptcy, collapse of commerce, and the failure of 'the paper securities of new, precarious, tottering power' as currency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secure property rights and trusted conventional credit are essential to a functioning state and economy; their systematic subversion brings fiscal ruin and social disorder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political rhetoric should avoid both gross adulation and humiliating flattery
rubrics_metrics.description: Dr. Price 'condemns... the practice of gross adulatory addresses to kings' but proposing to call the king 'Servant of the People' is 'not very soothing' and may be insulting rather than complimentary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public addresses should be measured: avoid fulsome flattery that corrupts, and avoid humiliating language that is not wholesome instruction—both can be counterproductive politically and morally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders and followers must each have appropriate capacities of judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: To be led otherwise than blindly, 'the followers must be qualified, if not for actors, at least for judges'; leaders must respect or fear those they conduct to secure sober propositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective representative government requires that leaders shape proposals suited to the tastes and capacities of their followers, and followers be capable of judging leadership; otherwise leaders will conform to ignorance or opportunism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unresisted, presumptuous change in peace is the real cause of national ruin
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'fresh ruins of France... are not the devastation of civil war: they are the sad, but instructive monuments of rash and ignorant counsel in time of profound peace.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many disastrous outcomes attributed to war are often the result of heedless reforms enacted without opposition during peaceful times; prudent caution and institutional resistance are protections against such ruin.
